description: This entry covers Current Research Frontiers in Phylogenetics as part of the fundamentals of phylogenetics. In this field, molecular clocks matters because mutations accumulating at roughly steady rates, dating divergences. It is taught at the Advanced level of the teaching ladder, building from first principles toward professional practice, with each concept defined before it is used.
overview: Phylogenetics is the field concerned with Reconstructing the tree of life: how species are related and how evolution actually happened. Current Research Frontiers in Phylogenetics belongs to its essential core. Concretely: Molecular clocks — mutations accumulating at roughly steady rates, dating divergences. And Bayesian phylogenetics — posterior probabilities on trees via MCMC sampling. Mastering this entry means being able to explain the topic in plain sentences, recognize it in real cases, and apply it alongside the neighboring ideas of the Advanced tier.
core_concepts: Molecular clocks: mutations accumulating at roughly steady rates, dating divergences.
Bayesian phylogenetics: posterior probabilities on trees via MCMC sampling.
key_laws: Molecular clock hypothesis: roughly constant substitution rates along lineages.
Long-branch attraction: the artifact pulling fast-evolving lineages together spuriously.
vocabulary: Clade: a complete branch including an ancestor and all descendants.
Node support: the statistical confidence in a branch.
methods: Sequence alignment: building the homologous columns trees need.
history: Phylogenetics descends from Darwin's 1859 single tree sketch; Hennig's 1960s cladistics formalized it, and DNA sequencing plus Felsenstein's likelihood methods made molecular trees the standard for life's history.
